bull_bear.body:
- Captive solar power across both manufacturing units - 3 MW + 4 MW DC at Guna and a 3 MW DC plant installed at Baddi on 27th March 2026 - giving a structurally lower and more predictable power cost baseline
- Guna solar has generated over 10 million units (10,054,321 KWH) of clean energy since installation, saving an estimated Rs. 8 crore at an average tariff of Rs. 8 per KWH
- Continuous machinery modernisation (LMW LC361 cards, RF LR9SX draw frame, Savio Proxima-L autoconers) delivering higher output, fewer stoppages and reduced operator dependency
- Low leverage - debt-equity ratio of 0.13 in FY 2025-26 against 0.16 the prior year
- Stable industrial relations, with 3,158 employees on rolls as on 31st March 2026 against 3,009 a year earlier
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Dependence on imported raw materials (PTA and MEG) — MD&A Risks and Concerns names this as the key concern: reliance on imported Purified Terephthalic Acid and Monoethylene Glycol exposes manufacturers to global price fluctuations, supply disruptions and currency volatility. The Threats section adds that the exposure runs back to crude oil and is made more acute by 'the war situation in oil producing countries', which sits directly on the Company's input cost line.
- Tariff disadvantage in key export markets — India faces tariff disadvantages in major export markets versus Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia, which enjoy preferential trade agreements with the EU and the US. Management states this reduces the price competitiveness of Indian MMF-based garments and fabrics - a structural handicap on the export book that no operational action can offset.
- Cheaper MMF imports compressing domestic price and utilisation — Management flags intense competition from cheaper imports, particularly from China, affecting domestic pricing and margins, and states that rising imports 'pose a threat to domestic manufacturers, impacting margins and capacity utilisation'. The Board's Report repeats that fabric imports from competing markets 'remained an active challenge for domestic players' during FY 2025-26.
- High energy and logistics costs; power tariff exposure at Baddi — High energy and logistics costs are called structural challenges against low-cost producers like China and Vietnam. Company-specific: the upward revision in state government electricity tariffs caused a steep increase in power costs at the Baddi plant, which the Company is answering with a 2.976 MW captive solar plant.
- Sustainability, recycling and traceability compliance burden — Environmental regulations and global buyers' rising expectations on sustainability, recycling and traceability add compliance pressure requiring significant investment, which management notes is difficult for smaller units to adopt quickly - a recurring cost of staying qualified with export buyers.
- Skill shortages and slow technology adoption — Skill shortages in advanced polymer processing, limited domestic innovation in high-performance fibres and slow adoption of modern technology are named as long-term risks. Management adds that addressing labour-related bottlenecks through skill development and investing in automation will be critical for sustaining growth.
- Thin profitability and a Negative credit-rating outlook — The MD&A ratio commentary shows the Company only returned to profit in FY 2025-26 after a loss the prior year, with net profit margin at 0.68% and return on net worth at 1.60%; ICRA's long-term rating of [ICRA]A- carries a Negative outlook as at 23rd September 2025. Little cushion absorbs a further input-cost or realisation shock.
- Concentration in a single activity and two manufacturing sites — All disclosed operations are specialised yarn spinning at just two units, Baddi (Himachal Pradesh) and Guna (Madhya Pradesh), with no subsidiary, JV or associate disclosed in the routed text - so an event at either site, or a downturn confined to MMF yarn, has nothing to be diversified against.

business.body: Deepak Spinners manufactures specialised yarns for the Indian man-made-fibre (MMF) textile chain, with the Board describing 'agile pricing strategies across specialized yarn segments' as the way it navigates competitive pressure. Operations run through spinning units at Baddi (Himachal Pradesh) and Guna (Madhya Pradesh), using blow room, carding, draw frame, ring frame and autoconer lines. The Company serves domestic textile demand and exports, and its cost position is being reshaped by captive solar power at both units.

business.title: Competitive strengths

outlook.body:
- Reinforce product positioning, optimise demand forecasting and execute agile pricing across specialised yarn segments to navigate competitive pressure from fabric imports
- Green-energy expansion across the manufacturing footprint - captive solar at both Guna and Baddi - to insulate operations from volatile state tariff structures and structurally lower the power cost baseline
- Resource optimisation and sustainable infrastructure as a continuing operational focus, aimed at energy self-reliance, a reduced carbon footprint and predictable power cost savings
- Continued emphasis on operational excellence in pursuit of sustainable growth and profitability
- Technology absorption through machinery replacement (LMW LC361 cards, RF LR9SX draw frame) for higher output, lower stoppages and reduced operator dependency
- Conserve cash for future growth plans - no dividend recommended for FY 2025-26 after considering the Company's financial position and growth plans
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Capex in FY 2025-26 was directed almost entirely at captive renewable power and machinery modernisation rather than at spinning capacity addition. At the Guna unit the 4 MW DC solar plant commissioned in FY 2024-25 completed its first full year of operation, taking Guna's captive solar to 3 MW + 4 MW DC; the plants together have generated over 10 million units (10,054,321 KWH), saving an estimated Rs. 8 crore at an average tariff of Rs. 8 per KWH and avoiding more than 8,000 tons of CO2, and currently generate roughly 5 lakh units of electricity a month. At Baddi, where the upward revision in state government electricity tariffs caused a steep increase in power costs, the Company installed a 3 MW DC solar plant within the premises on 27th March 2026 (it had generated 9,960 KWH by 31st March 2026, with meaningful generation only from the next year); the Board's Report describes this as a 2.976 MW solar power plant installed at the Baddi unit in FY 2026-27, while the MD&A - written earlier in the same report - says it 'is being installed'. The Company states a capital investment of Rs. 7.15 crore on the Baddi solar plant and other energy conservation measures. Other Baddi energy work included new variable frequency drives on the induced-draft and forced-draft fans of the 6 tonne-per-hour Thermax boiler, replacement of an old Atlas Copco GA-75+ compressor with an energy-efficient Kaeser CSDX 145T, LED street lighting, thermal insulation of steam pipelines and acrylic sunlight sheets on godowns. Under technology absorption, Guna Works replaced four LMW C1/3 carding machines with four LMW LC361 cards and one G5/1 with an RF LR9SX draw frame, adding production capacity per machine, reducing stoppages and operator dependency and lifting downstream productivity; a 200 kilolitre-per-day underground rainwater-harvesting tank at the 4 MW Guna solar site serves the G1 and G2 units. No new spinning line, greenfield plant or capacity-addition project is disclosed in the routed text.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Global fashion and textile markets are shifting steadily from cotton to man-made fibres on better durability, versatility and cost efficiency, creating strong long-term demand for Indian MMF products
- Strong domestic consumption, growth in organised retail and the rise of e-commerce support long-term expansion of the Indian MMF industry
- Government policy support - the PLI scheme and PM MITRA parks - plus ongoing investment in modern machinery is expected to enhance scale, efficiency and competitiveness in coming years
- Global brands diversifying sourcing away from single-country dependence positions India as a preferred sourcing destination; management cites an 'increasing preference for reliable sourcing partners'
- Growth in technical textiles, sportswear, performance fabrics and recycled fibres is likely to create new opportunities for value addition
- Improving global demand underpins management's optimism on the long-term prospects of the textile sector
- Margin lever: captive solar power at Guna (full first year of the 4 MW plant) and now Baddi, offsetting the steep increase in Baddi power costs from the upward revision in state government tariffs
- Headwinds management expects to persist: tariff disadvantages versus Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia, raw-material (PTA/MEG) price volatility, and sustainability-compliance requirements
- Cheaper MMF imports, particularly from China, continue to pressure domestic pricing, margins and capacity utilisation
- Overall medium-term outlook described as 'stable to optimistic', driven by modernisation, innovation and expanding domestic and export demand
